name: Zul
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only survey/classification refs (Decker & Aregbesola 2022, Blench 2014); no grammar or phonology of Zul located

new_statements.quote: Zul has two basic tones, H & L. Examples of lexical contrast purely through tone are extremely rare. [...] In a few cases, the presence of palatals and labials produces phonetic rising and falling tones. These are treated as sequences of vowels to avoid expanding the toneme inventory. [...] In a small number of tri- and quadrisyllabic words where the last two syllables are high, the second tone is lowered, a downstep is heard. [p. 6] || Zul has a relatively simple system of two tone-heights with occasional downstep appearing in longer words. However, tonal distinctions play an important role in the verbal system. [p. ii]
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2014. An introduction to Zul. Ms., Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, 30 pp. (draft circulated for comment, 13 November 2014).
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Tones, p. 6 (first quote); Abstract, p. ii (second quote)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., text layer, Acrobat Distiller, dated 13 Nov 2014; title page: 'An introduction to Zul... Presented at BICCL 7, Hamburg 12-14 Sept 2013... DRAFT CIRCULATED FOR COMMENT'). Both quoted passages are there verbatim: §2.3 Tones on printed p. 6 (PDF page 9) reads 'Zul has two basic tones, H & L. Examples of lexical contrast purely through tone are extremely rare.'... 'In a few cases, the presence of palatals and labials produces phonetic rising and falling tones. These are treated as sequences of vowels to avoid expanding the toneme inventory.'... 'In a small number of tri- and quadrisyllabic words where the last two syllables are high, the second tone is lowered, a downstep is hea…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zul is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with occasional downstep and no contour tones; tone carries grammatical load in the pronoun/TAM system. The sketch says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tonal: rare lexical tone minimal pairs (bì 'give' / bí 'language, mouth'; ɓálì 'cowpeas' / ɓàlí 'to tie'), phonetic rising/falling tones from palatal/labial glides reanalysed as vowel sequences, and downstep in some HH-final tri-/quadrisyllables that 'does not occur in all lexical items with this tonal formula'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in citation forms of a 2012 wordlist plus pronoun paradigms; no phrase-level prosody, no instrumental data; the author calls it a 'basic phonology sketch' from three days of elicitation.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2014 describes the Zul of the villages around Zul/Zulgami (Bauchi and Toro LGAs), elicited in Jos from Dangana Adamu and colleagues in April 2012; it equates Zul with the 'Barma/Mbaram' of older sources while noting Mbaram may be a related dialect. Decker & Aregbesola 2022 distinguish Zul-Nasira and Zul-Botkile/Binzula varieties (both assigned to zlu by Glottolog). No dialect-specific stress information exists. The earlier scan note ('only survey/classification refs') was wrong in one respect: Blench 2014 is a 30-page grammar sketch with a phonology section, not a survey; it simply never mentions stress.
